name: The App Interviewer
oneLiner: Turns one plain-English request into the correct sequence of API calls, chains their outputs, and executes them against the live app.
lead: The app exposes an HTTP API — `create_conversation`, `search_users`, `list_documents`, and so on. This agent lets you drive it in natural language: describe the outcome, and an LLM plans the ordered list of endpoint calls, wires each step's response into the next, executes them with a bearer token, and reports every step's result.
chore: Driving the API by hand means knowing each endpoint's exact name, its request body shape, and how to feed one call's response into the next. A single wish like 'create a conversation about X and share it with Jordan' is three separate, carefully chained requests. Testers and analysts who aren't developers can't build them by hand.
instead: Write one sentence. The agent has an LLM plan the call sequence, threads each step's output into the next via `$prev` references, executes them against the live API, and logs what each returned.
whyItMatters: It turns a developer-only API into something anyone on the team can drive with a sentence, so testing and everyday tasks stop bottlenecking on scarce technical hands.

howItWorks.step: Sends your request to an LLM with a strict instruction to return only a JSON array of API actions and their parameters.
howItWorks.explain: This is the **planning** step: the model's only job is to translate one sentence into a machine-executable `ActionStep[]`, so the code treats its reply as data, not prose. Models routinely wrap JSON in Markdown fences even when told not to, so it **strips ```json and ``` fences defensively** before parsing rather than assuming clean output. The `try/catch` converts a malformed reply into an explicit, truncated error (`slice(0, 200)`) — that truncation keeps a runaway multi-KB response from flooding the log while still showing enough to diagnose. A parse failure **aborts the whole run before any API call fires**, which is the safe default: better no actions than a half-understood plan executed against the live app.

howItWorks.step: Threads outputs between steps: for 'create a conversation and share it,' the plan marks where step one's returned ID drops into steps two and three.
howItWorks.explain: This is the **data-flow glue** that makes multi-step plans work: the LLM can't know a conversation's ID at planning time, so it writes the placeholder `$prev.conversationId` and this resolver fills it in at run time from actual results. The common case is special-cased to read the **most recent** result (`prevResults.length - 1`), and it tolerates API shape drift by trying `conversationId` first and falling back to `id` — different endpoints name the field differently. The final `|| ''` means an unresolvable reference degrades to an **empty string rather than `undefined`**, which surfaces downstream as an obvious bad-parameter API error instead of a silent `undefined` crash. Only string values starting with `$prev` are touched; every literal parameter passes through untouched.

howItWorks.step: Executes each step in order against the live API, substituting cross-step references as it goes.
howItWorks.explain: A **closed dispatch** — the `switch` is an allow-list, and the `default` throws on any action name the LLM invents, so a hallucinated verb can never reach the live API. The `share_conversation` case does the real work: it maps each planned recipient through `resolveUser` (name → real account) and **encodes the role as a number** (`edit → 1`, anything else → `0`/read-only), so the safer permission is the default when the role is unspecified or unrecognized. It **guards against sharing with nobody** — if every name fails to resolve, it throws rather than firing a share with an empty user list, which would either error opaquely or silently share with no one. `params.users || []` tolerates a plan that omitted the users array entirely.

howItWorks.step: For a share-with-a-named-person step, first resolves the name against the directory to a real account before issuing the share.
howItWorks.explain: Sharing with the wrong person is the exact bug this must not create, so matching is **strict-first**: the whole candidate list is scanned for an **exact** display-name equality before any fuzzy logic runs, so 'John Smith' never binds to 'John Smithson' when the exact person exists. Only if no exact hit is found does it fall to a **case-insensitive contains** pass as a convenience. The search *term* is deliberately looser than the match — it takes only the part before the first comma (`split(',')[0]`) so a 'Last, First' input still returns candidates from a directory that indexes on last name, while the equality check still uses the full original string. Every field read is defensively chained (`displayName || userName || name`, `email || mail || userEmail`) to survive directory-payload shape differences, and it returns `null` — not a guess — when nothing matches, so the caller can refuse to share rather than pick someone arbitrary.

howItWorks.step: Prints a running log of each step's result, then persists the full plan and every response to a JSON file.
howItWorks.explain: This is **display-only** — it never mutates state, it condenses each raw response into one readable console line so you can follow the plan live (the full raw payload still lands in the JSON report). Each branch is written to **not throw on a partial response**: `result.answer || ''` before `.match`/`.slice` guards against a missing answer, and the word count uses `?.length || 0` so a null match reads as 0 rather than crashing. The `send_message` branch **truncates the answer to 200 chars** so a multi-paragraph reply doesn't wall the terminal, and `search_users` **caps the printout at 10 people** for the same reason while still reporting the true total count. The `default` branch pretty-prints anything unrecognized and hard-caps it at 1000 chars — a safety net so a new action type still logs something bounded.

examples.caption: One sentence, three chained calls
examples.input: Request: 'Create a conversation asking about renewable-energy projects and share it with Rivera, Sam.'
examples.output: A three-step plan runs: a conversation is created, the question is sent and answered, Sam Rivera is resolved in the directory, and the conversation is shared read-only — each step logged as it completes.

examples.caption: A single lookup
examples.output: One directory-search call returns a short list of matching people with names and email addresses.

examples.caption: Reading feature flags
examples.output: One call to the settings endpoint returns the on/off flags controlling which features are currently live.

underHood.heading: Plans the call sequence
underHood.whenRuns: First, the moment you submit a request.
underHood.output: A JSON array of API actions to run, in order, produced by the LLM.

underHood.heading: Chains step outputs
underHood.input: A step's parameters, which may contain a placeholder like `$prev.conversationId`.
underHood.output: The placeholder substituted with the real value from an earlier step, so step two can use the ID step one returned.

underHood.heading: Calls the app's API
underHood.whenRuns: Once per step in the plan.
underHood.input: The resolved action name and parameters.
underHood.output: An HTTPS request to the app's API, authorized with a bearer token, and the parsed response.

underHood.heading: Resolves names before sharing
underHood.whenRuns: Only for steps that share with a named person.
underHood.output: That person's real account, resolved against the directory — exact match first, contains match as fallback.

underHood.heading: Persists the run
underHood.input: The full plan plus every step's result.
underHood.output: One timestamped JSON file capturing exactly what was requested, what ran, and what came back.

prerequisites: Node ≥ 18 and a terminal (macOS/Linux shell or Windows PowerShell).
A reachable instance of the app's API to target, plus a bearer token authorized to call it.
Directory search must be reachable through that same API, since any share-with-a-named-person step resolves people by name.
An AI key (defaults to a Google model) — a sentence has to be planned into an ordered call sequence before anything executes.

steps.label: Install Node.js — the runtime the agent runs on.
steps.cmd:
# macOS (with Homebrew):
brew install node

# or download the LTS installer from nodejs.org, then check it worked:
node -v   # should print v18 or higher
steps.why: The agent is a TypeScript program; Node executes it. Install once per machine.
steps.firstRun: Only needed on a fresh machine.

steps.label: Clone the agent code and install its dependencies.
steps.why: `npm install` pulls the agent's dependencies — the AI client and the HTTPS request helper it calls the API with.
steps.rerun: No-op once installed, unless the dependency list changed.

steps.label: Set the target environment (environment variables).
steps.cmd:
export APP_API_URL_DEV=https://dev.your-app.example.com
export APP_API_TOKEN_DEV=your-bearer-token
export GOOGLE_API_KEY=your-ai-key
export APP_MODEL=gpt5   # optional, this is the default
steps.why: The base URL and token select the environment's API and authorize it. The AI key is what plans your one-sentence request into an ordered call sequence.

steps.label: State the outcome in one sentence and run it.
steps.cmd:
npx ts-node agents/app-api-agent.ts --env dev \
  --prompt "Create a conversation asking about renewable-energy projects and share it with Rivera, Sam"
steps.why: `--env` selects the environment; `--prompt` is your sentence. The agent plans it (create, then ask, then share), resolves 'Rivera, Sam' against the directory, and executes every step against the live API.
steps.firstRun: Nothing is cached — it plans and executes live against the real environment every time.
steps.rerun: Identical each time: a brand-new conversation is created and, if sharing was requested, a fresh share call goes out.

steps.label: Open the run record.
steps.why: The saved file holds the LLM's step-by-step plan plus the raw response from every step — proof of exactly what ran, in what order.

inputs.name: --prompt "..."
inputs.desc: One natural-language sentence describing the outcome you want.

inputs.name: environment variables
inputs.desc: The API URL and bearer token for the chosen environment, plus the AI key.

outputs.name: console log
outputs.desc: Each step in the plan printed as it runs, with a one-line result summary.

outputs.name: ApiAgent_<env>_<timestamp>.json
outputs.desc: The full plan the LLM produced plus every step's raw response, timestamped for the record.

runbook.rerun: No idempotency: running the same prompt twice creates two conversations, and if the prompt includes a share step, fires the share twice. Treat every run as a fresh, live action against the real environment, not a safe replay.
runbook.integrate: The fastest way to smoke-test the API after a deploy — one sentence exercises a whole chain of real calls (create, ask, share) instead of three hand-built requests. Feed it a prompt list from a CI job to catch a broken chain before a person does.

video.caption: A 3-minute screen recording: type one sentence, watch it turn into a chain of real service-counter calls.
script: Open a terminal and say: 'This agent turns one plain sentence into the right sequence of API calls. Watch.'
Run `node -v` to confirm Node is installed; one line on what Node is.
Run `npm install` (or note it's already done); explain it's grabbing the AI client and the request helper.
Show the three `export` lines for the URL, token, and AI key; say 'this is the only place environment-specific detail lives.'
Type the run command with a one-sentence prompt: 'Create a conversation about renewable-energy projects and share it with Rivera, Sam.'
Narrate as the plan prints: three steps — create, ask, share.
Point out the moment it resolves 'Rivera, Sam' against the company directory before sharing.
Show each step's result line appear in the terminal as it completes.
Open the saved `.json`; show the plan and the raw responses sitting side by side.
Close: 'One sentence just did what used to take a developer three manual calls.'
